assumption: More automation necessarily produces better operations
evidence_for: EV-076 (no sponsor measures latency so manual review has no demonstrated quality advantage); EV-082 (revoked-EIN dollars 0.082% shows deterministic screens catch the measurable failure class); EV-136 (opex per grant $61 Fidelity vs $162 Vanguard vs $474 NPT with automation-heavy affiliates at the low end)
counterarguments: EV-153 (AI-on-existing-workflow result was an artefact); EV-113 (unconstrained AI creates risk in 13 of 16 failure modes); automation at scale amplifies a single misconfiguration (FM-01); twin shows exception volume not automation is the bottleneck
competing_explanations: Lower opex per grant at Fidelity/DAFgiving360 may reflect affiliate cost allocation (EV-134) and small average grants not automation
causal_mechanism: Automation lowers cost and variance only where the rule is explicit and its inputs are fresh; where judgment or stale data is involved it moves error rather than removing it
falsification_criteria: An automated process with independent QA shows higher escaped-error rate than the manual baseline it replaced
reconsideration_triggers: GAP-004 human error baseline measured; first QA sample of deterministic approvals (Area D monthly sample)

assumption: AI should replace every existing human activity
evidence_for: None in repository supports universal replacement; EV-102 (no entity documents AI in approval); EV-090 (personal manager liability under §4966/4967)
counterarguments: Outcome model assigns 33 of 81 decision types to H; 16 of 80 legacy activities retained as human-accountable (activity-classification.md); law places knowing-manager liability on people (EV-090)
competing_explanations: AI adoption pressure is vendor-side (EV-103: AI in 29.1% of vendor vs 13.3% of sponsor postings)
causal_mechanism: Accountability attaches to persons and fiduciaries; delegation to a model does not transfer liability
falsification_criteria: A regulator or court accepts model-made sponsor decisions as satisfying sponsor control and manager duties
reconsideration_triggers: Final §4966/6033 guidance (GAP-008); any IRS ruling on automated grant approval

assumption: All grant decisions can be automated
evidence_for: EV-079/EV-081 (~7-8.5% of grants by count need review on core proxy so ~92% are routine candidates); EV-082; DD-004
counterarguments: EV-080/EV-079 core proxy 11.61% of dollars; ER and equivalency determinations are judgments (REG map); EV-097 discretionary holds are board judgments; prohibited-benefit has no bright-line definition (regulatory map §12)
competing_explanations: Routine share could be lower if undocumented reputational screens are applied (EV-097)
causal_mechanism: Statute excepts listed public charities (§4966(c)(1)) making the routine class rule-decidable; non-routine classes require facts not in structured data
falsification_criteria: Shadow-mode replay shows deterministic rules cannot reproduce ≥95% of a partner's historical routine approvals or human review catches material issues in the routine class
reconsideration_triggers: Q-N03 / GAP-001 study; GAP-034 shadow test results

assumption: A single platform must own every financial function
evidence_for: Incumbent integrated stacks (EV-023 FMR provides record-keeping; EV-044 RCF→Ren 98% fee)
counterarguments: EV-116 (losses only where one operator held unsegregated funds); EV-119 (all DAF-tech exits went to consolidators creating concentration); DD-008 (custody and rails partnered); regulatory map §14 (holding funds triggers money transmission)
competing_explanations: Integration may be valued for accountability simplicity rather than capability
causal_mechanism: Splitting custody and rails from decisioning limits blast radius and licensing exposure while event contracts preserve coherence
falsification_criteria: Partnered custody/rail integration produces reconciliation breaks or latency materially worse than integrated incumbents in pilot
reconsideration_triggers: Break rates measured in Phase 4; a partner rail outage longer than RTO

assumption: Lower headcount always means lower risk
evidence_for: EV-128 (bank-change callback controls are people-dependent at incumbents); twin: capacity -40% stress produces 346 days over SLA
counterarguments: Twin shows single complex-asset specialist and surge breaches are concentration risks; segregation of duties needs ≥2 people per sensitive function; automation complacency (FM-04); fewer people means fewer independent observers of anomalies
competing_explanations: Risk may fall with fewer manual touch points (fewer keying errors and insider opportunities)
causal_mechanism: Risk depends on controls and independent observation not headcount; removing people removes both error sources and detection capacity
falsification_criteria: Incident data over 24 months shows no increase in undetected-error duration after headcount reduction
reconsideration_triggers: Any incident detected by external party rather than internal control; specialist attrition event

assumption: Every existing compliance step is legally required
evidence_for: Some steps are (REG map 50 legal obligations)
counterarguments: Regulatory map: 8 risk controls and 7 conventions commonly mistaken for law (BSA/AML program; §4944; payout minimums; callbacks; Form 8283 as appraisal endorsement); activity census 14 conventions
competing_explanations: Sponsors may retain steps for reputational or insurer reasons not law
causal_mechanism: Liability aversion plus absence of shared eligibility data sustains blanket review (industry report §3 mixed classification)
falsification_criteria: Counsel confirms a step classified as convention is legally required in a state of operation
reconsideration_triggers: Counsel review of regulatory-applicability-matrix.csv; new state law

evidence_for: EV-077 (sponsors advertise 2-10 day latencies); Daffy growth (EV-058 vendor claim)
counterarguments: EV-114 (93% value AI transparency; 39.8% uneasy about data use); EV-015 (median account pays out 9% over 3 years — most donors are not latency-bound); EV-125 complaints concern payout rules and lost checks not speed per se; nonprofits not donors bear latency cost (EV-074)
competing_explanations: Speed may be a proxy for certainty and visibility
causal_mechanism: Donor utility comes from tax timing certainty trust and visibility; speed matters most to recipients
falsification_criteria: Conjoint or pilot data show speed dominates trust/visibility/fees in DAF choice

assumption: Advisors will accept a platform that reduces their control
counterarguments: EV-027 (CIAP 46.9% of Fidelity investments adviser-managed and rising); EV-068 adviser fee layer; RCF/Ren spine distribution (industry report §2.2); EV-092 proposed reg would treat adviser as donor-advisor
competing_explanations: Advisors may accept reduced control if fee and relationship preserved
causal_mechanism: Advisor revenue is AUM-linked; a platform that disintermediates investment management removes the incentive to place assets
falsification_criteria: Advisor pilot shows placement rates unaffected by loss of investment-management role
reconsideration_triggers: Final §4966 regs adopting adviser-as-donor-advisor rule; advisor pilot conversion data

assumption: A new sponsoring organization is preferable to supplying infrastructure
evidence_for: 09 model: B steady-state margin 85% at 100k accounts [S]; optimistic ramp peak capital $2.5m [S]
counterarguments: 09 calibrated B ramp peak capital $12.8m and negative at year 5 [S]; EV-118 no entrant shows optimistic path; 10-market comparison A and B never rank first; EV-019 sponsor exits rare so incumbents persist; EV-122 data access closed
competing_explanations: B's economics hinge on asset acquisition rate which is unmeasured
causal_mechanism: Sponsor value comes from distribution and trust which accrue slowly; infrastructure can reach existing books faster
falsification_criteria: A design-partner sponsor-of-record arrangement fails and an owned sponsor reaches $2bn faster than calibrated path
reconsideration_triggers: CAC and asset-acquisition data from Phase 6 advisor pilot

assumption: DD-004 deterministic approval of routine grants is safe
evidence_for: EV-082; EV-045 (RCF: Charity Check adequate for >98% of historical grants); Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance; DD-004
counterarguments: EV-097 (reputational holds outside rules); account-takeover fraud may present as routine grants to real charities with hijacked bank accounts (FM-12); regulator might view no-touch approval as weak sponsor control (FM-10)
competing_explanations: Two-person review may catch fraud and benefit cases not captured by structured data
causal_mechanism: Statutory exception plus fresh IRS/OFAC data plus payee verification covers the legal risk; fraud risk is addressed by payment gate not grant review
falsification_criteria: Monthly QA sample of deterministic approvals finds material issues at a rate above the agreed tolerance
reconsideration_triggers: QA sample results; IRS guidance on sponsor control; first fraud loss through routine path

evidence_for: PoC journey: ledger identity holds across returns and holds (59 tests); EV-037 / EV-121 history loss and portability gaps
counterarguments: Operational complexity (schema evolution replay side effects FM-09); team skills; incumbents run CRUD successfully at scale
competing_explanations: Benefits could be obtained with CRUD plus audit tables
causal_mechanism: Replayable history makes audit lineage portability and policy back-testing cheap; costs arise in schema evolution
falsification_criteria: Phase 2-3 engineering cost of event versioning exceeds benefit measured in audit/export effort
reconsideration_triggers: Phase 3 engineering telemetry; first schema migration

assumption: Human exception rate of ~8% of grants and determinations are reusable
evidence_for: EV-081 (7-8.5% per grant core proxy); EV-025 (12.5 grants per recipient at Fidelity → clustering)
counterarguments: Proxy measures recipients not observed review (EV-079); broad proxy 17-31% (EV-081); misses donor-controlled supporting orgs; reuse legality across sponsors unclear (API-12 issue)
competing_explanations: Actual rate could be much lower (standing rules) or higher (reputational screens)
causal_mechanism: Exceptions concentrate in recipient classes; recipient-level determinations amortize
falsification_criteria: Measured partner exception rate outside 3-15% or reuse factor <1.5

evidence_for: EV-106 (~$0.45 vs ~$83); 09 model inference 0.3% of cost; x10 sensitivity swing 2.7%
counterarguments: Agentic multi-step runs and evaluation/monitoring costs larger than per-call inference; price changes; human review of AI output costs dominate
competing_explanations: Total AI cost includes evaluation datasets agent owners and incident handling (4 FTE agent ownership in model)
causal_mechanism: Per-token prices are small relative to loaded labor; cost sits in supervision
falsification_criteria: Measured AI run cost per completed outcome exceeds 5% of staff cost per outcome

assumption: Conventions carry no hidden risk value
counterarguments: Candidates with possible undocumented risk value: (a) two-person review of routine grants may catch account-takeover patterns; (b) paper checks add friction against fast fraud; (c) month-end close forces periodic human review that catches drift; (d) phone callbacks verifying charity bank changes (EV-128 shows few sponsors publish them); (e) welcome mail as out-of-band identity confirmation; (f) wholesaler visits as relationship signal
competing_explanations: These conventions may persist simply from habit (industry report §3)
causal_mechanism: Some conventions double as detective controls; removing them without replacement removes detection
falsification_criteria: Each candidate's detective function is either reproduced by a designed control (CTL-004 CTL-005 CTL-015 CTL-033) or shown to have caught nothing in partner history
reconsideration_triggers: Fraud incident through a path where a removed convention would have acted

assumption: Year-end surge (not average) sizes the human organization
evidence_for: Twin baseline: 34 days over SLA in December at 100k accounts [S]
counterarguments: Surge multiplier x3 is assumed; recurring grants (EV-033 38%) may smooth load; pre-clearing could absorb
competing_explanations: December concentration of contributions rather than grants may dominate
causal_mechanism: Peaked arrivals against fixed capacity create backlog
falsification_criteria: Partner daily grant series shows December peak <1.5x average or exceptions not concentrated

assumption: Model C buyers exist at ~$300 per account
evidence_for: EV-044 ($19.23m for 25,824 accounts ≈ $745/account single related-party contract); EV-060 Endaoment partner tiers
counterarguments: EV-122/123 data access closed; EV-119 consolidator lock-in; incumbent contracts renew; no willingness-to-pay data (GAP-014); small sponsors cannot pay (EV-013)
competing_explanations: Sponsors may prefer incumbents for liability and continuity
causal_mechanism: Administrators are paid a share of fundholder fees; a cheaper credible operator could capture share at renewal
falsification_criteria: No sponsor ≥20k accounts signs a paid design-partner agreement within 12 months
reconsideration_triggers: Phase 4 commercial outcomes; incumbent price cuts

assumption: The advisor channel prefers embedded APIs
evidence_for: Distribution via wealth platforms (industry report §2.2; DFX portals); TIFIN Give advisor stack
counterarguments: Advisors use custodian/wealth-platform UIs and may prefer the platform's native DAF; integration burden on firms; EV-122 shows firms restrict automation
competing_explanations: Firms want DAF assets on their own platform for fee capture rather than API convenience
causal_mechanism: Advisor adoption follows fee preservation and workflow integration inside existing tools
falsification_criteria: ≥3 wealth-firm partners decline API integration in favor of white-label portals

assumption: Agents cannot cause authoritative state changes because tools are absent
evidence_for: PoC types: AgentOutput has no approving constructor; INV-A1..A8 tests pass
counterarguments: Indirect influence: agent-drafted dossiers anchor human approvers (FM-04); agent flags can be suppressed by not running; prompt injection can bias proposals (FM-14)
competing_explanations: Humans may rubber-stamp agent recommendations making them de facto decisions
causal_mechanism: Structural absence prevents direct effect but not persuasion
falsification_criteria: Reviewer override rate on agent-dossier recommendations <2% over a quarter (complacency signal)

assumption: Smallest responsible organization ~21 FTE at 1k and ~104 at 100k accounts
counterarguments: 23 of 30 parameters assumed; loaded cost per FTE swing 95%; complex-asset and exception pools linear
competing_explanations: Outsourcing (OCIO non-cash processor fractional counsel) could lower in-house FTE
causal_mechanism: Fixed accountability floor plus linear specialist pools
falsification_criteria: Measured handling times differ from assumed by >2x
